Porsche Mission S Aims to Reinterpret the Supercar for the Future: Mid-Engine, Fewer Screens, ICE
46 photos
Photo: Porsche AG
As promised and leaked before the unveiling event, the Porsche Mission S is a concept car aimed to preview the future of the supercar for the German brand. An eventual production model will not be electric, that’s for sure.
Porsche has a mission to come out of the woods of decaying profits and sales, and it’s called ‘ Sportwagenschmiede 2035 .’ Yep, Germans love these long and hard-to-pronounce words, that’s for sure! This summer we went with the family on vacation in Germany and we came back home not remembering even one place where we went to because of these difficult words…
Anyway, Porsche is just like that: you can’t pinpoint the exact name, but you know the experience was great. Luckily, they do know that when it comes to models and concepts, the name should be easy to understand and remember. Meet the Mission S , with the ‘S’ standing either for that long German word or, easier to remember, for ‘supercar.’
This is basically their manifesto concept car for “the brand's evolved design identity” and what’s coming soon above the 911 series – a new flagship sports car with a mid-engine platform and not fully electrified. Unfortunately, the speculation about the flat-eight engine has not been confirmed just yet because the company hasn’t revealed any technical specifications; thus we don’t know any performance figures, pricing, or a production timeline for the new sports car.
Instead, they talked about all other things. First, the location: the new prototype was presented on a pier in Queens, New York, with a view of the Manhattan skyline beyond. This is where the first picture of a mid-engined Porsche 550 Spyder was taken back in 1953. The Porsche Mission S “provides a glimpse of the ideas and design features that will shape Porsche in the coming years,” explains Michael Leiters, Chairman of the Executive Board of Porsche AG .
“At the same time, the Mission S represents a mid-engined super sports car platform positioned above the 911 – not as a one-off hypercar, but as a permanent and versatile addition to our customer offering,” adds Leiters. So, at least we know that a series-production model is coming after this concept, just like it happened with the Porsche Mission E from 2015 and its subsequent alter-ego in production, the Porsche Taycan, which landed in 2019.
Hopefully, this time around we’re not going to wait four more years to see the production version, as the Porsche Mission S looks production-ready with just a few modifications. The design is typical for Porsche but in order to set it apart from the 911, we can easily see a long-tail style, with Porsche claiming influences from the 917 (the fan-like cooling element above the enginee), GT1, and especially the 959 for the exterior.
Inside, Porsche is adapting to the ‘screenless’ current that has emerged after automakers bathed their cars in pillar-to-pillar displays that crashed and left people stranded with no access to simple functions like AC controls.
So, the Mission S takes cues from the 550 Spyder and 356 instead, and physical controls and switches are a big part of the experience, although they also combine analog and digital elements like the reworked Sport Chrono clock or the five round analog gauges that have digital displays behind them, creating an interesting 3D-like effect. There’s no center display – just a retractable smartphone holder with MagSafe technology.
